deep.reconstruction:
Folio 70r is mostly non-mathematical. It contains three layers.

(1) A heavily corrected pencil draft of a letter to Riemann's father ('Lieber Vater!'), dated 'Göttingen, den 28sten März 1855'. Riemann says he has at last reached the point where he can make his (soon) return journey. He hopes to be in Lüneburg by Thursday evening, where his family then lived, and to talk things over with his father. He would have written right after the end of his lectures on the 13th (his winter-semester 1854/55 course, presumably the one on partial differential equations whose heat-conduction notes appear on the previous folio), but he had hoped every day to be able to leave.

(2) A draft passage on physics: 'Bei der Anwendung dieses Gesetzes auf die Rückstandsbildung in der Leydener Flasche musste ich, da Angaben über die Dimensionen des Apparats fehlten, annehmen, daß die Dimensionen derselben gegen den Abstand der Belegungen als unendlich groß betrachtet werden dürften, welche Annahme in der That bei [Kohlrausch's] beiden Bedingungen erfüllt wurde. Aber ich habe ... fast gleichzeitig, Herr Professor Weber und Kirchhoff darauf aufmerksam ...'
- This concerns Riemann's 1854 theory of the residual charge (elektrischer Rückstand) in a Leyden jar. In it the dielectric 'resists' holding electricity with a finite force, so the problem reduces to a one-dimensional diffusion-type problem. That is exactly the half-space/slab heat problem treated on the previous folio, u_t = a^2 u_xx with solution C·erfc(x/(2a√t)).
- The assumption that the plate dimensions are infinite compared with the separation of the coatings is what makes the problem one-dimensional (a plane slab).
- He notes the assumption held for Kohlrausch's experiments. The draft continues with a reference to Weber and Kirchhoff, who had drawn attention to something at almost the same time. This fits the known episode in which Riemann's residual-charge paper was withdrawn from Poggendorff's Annalen in 1855.

(3) A bibliographic note: [W. Weber], 'Elektrodynamische Maassbestimmungen, insbesondere Widerstandsmessungen', Abhandlungen der k. sächs. Ges. d. Wiss. 1852, I, p. 293; Poggendorff's Annalen Bd 78, p. 506.

(4) In the lower half there are very faint pencil calculations, rational-function manipulations in a variable x. They contain fractions such as x/(1+x), (1+x)/(x(1-x)) and expressions apparently involving square roots of 1-x and of x.
- They are too faint to reconstruct line by line. My inference, not a reading: by content they appear to be scratch work for the quadratic transformations of Gauss's hypergeometric series on the next folio. That folio uses arguments such as 4x/(1+x)^2, ((1-√(1-x))/(1+√(1-x)))^2 and (1-√(1-x))/2, and substitutions such as z(1-z)/((1+x)^2-4xz) = y^2.
- The elementary identities behind such substitutions are 1 - 4x/(1+x)^2 = ((1-x)/(1+x))^2 and the like.
- No complete derivation can be stated with certainty from this page alone.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed. The faint calculations are not legible enough to check step by step.

The bibliographic data for the Poggendorff reference (Bd 78, S. 506) is uncertain in the reading and may not match the cited Weber paper. Weber's resistance measurements appeared in Pogg. Ann. Bd 82 (1851), so either the reading or Riemann's citation may be off.

results.what: Reduction of residual-charge formation in a Leyden jar to a one-dimensional diffusion problem by treating the plates as infinite compared with the dielectric thickness
results.modern_name: Dielectric absorption / relaxation modelled by a 1-D diffusion equation (plane-slab approximation)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1854 Göttingen Naturforscherversammlung paper on the distribution of tension electricity in ponderable bodies), with experiments by R. Kohlrausch (1854)

results.what: Faint scratch algebra apparently supporting quadratic transformations of the hypergeometric function (argument 4x/(1+x)^2 etc.)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a biographical draft letter to his father plus a note on his known 1854 residual-charge theory and its dispute with Kohlrausch, Weber and Kirchhoff. Biographically interesting, but the episode is known from Riemann's correspondence and Werke. The faint mathematics is illegible scratch work tied to standard hypergeometric transformations.

checkable.asserts: Elementary identity underlying the quadratic substitution z = 4x/(1+x)^2 used on the adjacent folio
The previous folio's half-space solution satisfies the heat (diffusion) equation used for the Leyden-jar residual-charge model
Identity behind the quadratic transformation with argument ((1-sqrt(1-x))/(1+sqrt(1-x)))^2 on the next folio

transcription_corrections: 'Lüneburg' is likely correct: Riemann's family lived in Lüneburg from 1855. The first occurrence in the machine transcript seems to be a duplicate of the second rather than a separate word.
'bei Kohlrausch's beiden Bedingungen' — the reading is uncertain. It may be 'bei Kohlrausch's beiden Flaschen' or a similar reference to Kohlrausch's experimental apparatus.
The heading of the bibliographic note likely reads '[Weber,] Elektrodynamische Maassbestimmungen, insbesondere Widerstandsmessungen'.
The faint lower calculations are not reliably transcribed. The given formulas such as 'x/(1+x) ... = x/(1+x) - 1/x' should be treated as conjectural.
